blocks.x: Yeah, okay. I just want to know your name first. What is it in here? George Kohler. For truth? That's your real name, no? Real name. And what's your other name? Your musical name? Sheik. Kid Sheik. How come they called you that in here?
I just used to dress in the Sheik clothes. I bought them suits with the arrows all around it. Arrows? Yeah, arrows on the back of the coat, side of the coat, pockets.
Made with thread? Sort of decorated with thread or something else sewed on them? How are you?

No, they're just arrows. Just put around this. You know, just one arrow here and one arrow. That was the time of Claude Gable suits come out. Well, they called them the Sheik. They used to have uptown pockets. You see, your pants was made like this, the pockets. They were a little more around in front. Yeah, like that. And they open on the top. Yeah. And I'm dropping that thing. Straight down. Uptown pockets, they call them. When were you born? I was born September 15, 1908. Where were you born? I was born on Maroney and Johnson.
Oh, good. Maroney and Johnson. Any of your family musicals?

No, my brother used to fool around with the horn, but he never played no jazz. He never played nothing. I would just try to fool with it. Well, he was a man then when he was trying to fool with it. He was all that. And I had the old horn around there and he was trying to do it. He was to blow it, you know. He wasn't blowing no pieces, but he could fill it up.
What about uncles and aunts and mother and daddy? None of them played? No, none of them played. None of them played. Hmm. None of them played. How did you get started yourself?

Well, it was by going by parties, yard parties. I'd go and used to have out in the old and the yards there, muddy yards, no pavement bands to be playing. Playing the blues and all that. I was quite young then. I just happened to go around and follow Wooden Joe and Chris Kelly, Sam Martin. I just wanted to play trumpet and got my old brass cornet. I was fooling around with brass all bent up. And what I did...
Just a second. Okay, you and your violins, I don't see why you don't. Well, anyway...

Yeah, I had that old beat up cornet it was. I just remember who I got that cornet from. I just remember who I got that cornet from. One old trumpet player, yeah, the cornet. I just remember it in there. It's been a good while. Anyway, I was around about ten or eleven years old then. And I fooled around and I could never blow the thing. I used to put a kazut in it. I used a mouthpiece to put a kazut. The mouthpiece to put a kazut? No, I'd put the kazut in the, you know, where the mouthpiece goes. You see, in the cornet. Did anybody else do that ever? I don't know. I mean, I did that and just blow, you know, but it wouldn't give it the cornet sound at this, you know, the kazut sound like that. And I just blow and that and just thought I was ready and saying, get with piano and drumming. And I had to close it in the cornet and then... ...and then... ...who around. And eventually I... ...I went and... ...around Wooden Joe. ...and then he'd tell me how to start me and how to fill the horn and blow. And blow and I'd follow him around. I used to follow Cuckoo. He used to play them yard parties too. Yeah. I followed him around the Pocorn yard, around there. A fellow got killed one night. He was playing there on Parker Street there, Paul and Maria. He used to have dance in that yard. He called it Pocorn yard. Was the guy that got killed the musician? Yeah. A fellow was a guitar player, they called him Hamp. He never played with no band but he was playing. Him and Walt and him used to play together. Blackburn. Yeah. He used to go around playing like fish fries, you know, and just be in the street playing like that. First and second. I mean he could play it too. He's the one that gave Walt a good start on that too. Nobody played with no band. Just go around and fish fry.
They have a lot of guys that just play piano and guitar and all kind of odd instruments serenading like that.

Yeah. Well that's all they did then. You see a fellow at two or three o'clock in the morning you'd hear a fellow passing the street playing his guitar, the blues, and a fellow people throwing nickels, dimes, you know, in that hole in there. And that's how they did. That's how they hustle.
I was wondering if you ever noticed, would they use a flat pick or would they use finger picks and thumb picks or all different kinds of things?

Well in that time, them fellows would use just their fingers. I see here lately now, I see them fellows with them picks, you know, them sideline picks, but them fellows way back then, I mean they'd just be picking that with their fingers. I mean they'd play it too. Old fellow Jim Lucas, he used to play some guitar, played banjo, but he played in bands and he used to play with Rene and all them fellas. Is he still around? Hmm? Is he still around? No, Jim Lucas, he died, he been dead. He was a good banjo player, guitar player too. He played most with all the bands.
You can hardly find a good blues picker like you used to. There's very few of them around.

Like guitar? Yeah. I believe Walter was about the only one, I mean, you know, picking the blues. He can play the blues there, he really can, you know, picking them on that style, you see. But most of them fellas that was playing during that time, I mean, they, they, now they had a fella down to him. I could play any of them, playing the guitar, blues and everything. He's crippled now. His name is Freddie. Freddie. He's a lottery vendor.
He lived down at Nightwars. Freddie. Freddie Gould. Freddie Gould. Freddie Gould. I mean, he'd play high school.

segments.title: How he got the name Kid Sheik: arrow suits
segments.summary: Asked his real and musical names, he explains he dressed in Sheik-style suits with arrows and uptown pockets.

segments.title: Birth in 1908 and non-musical family
segments.summary: Born September 15, 1908 at Maroney and Johnson; only his brother fooled with a horn, no relatives played.

segments.title: Learning cornet around yard parties and Wooden Joe
segments.summary: As a boy of ten or eleven he followed yard-party bands of Wooden Joe, Chris Kelly and Cuckoo, played a bent cornet with a kazoo in it, and Wooden Joe showed him how to blow.

segments.title: Pocorn yard, a killing, and street guitarists
segments.summary: He recalls dances at Pocorn yard where a guitarist named Hamp was killed, and guitarists who played fish fries and serenaded the streets for nickels and dimes.

segments.title: Guitar and banjo players: Jim Lucas, Walter, Freddie Gould
segments.summary: He discusses fingerpicking style, banjo player Jim Lucas who played with Rene, the blues picker Walter, and the crippled guitarist Freddie Gould.
